indicaciones_tradicionales: impotence and premature ejaculation due to Kidney Yang deficiency
infertility due to Cold in the uterus or Yang deficiency
low back pain and weak knees
joint pain from Wind-Dampness with Kidney deficiency
irregular menstruation with Cold and lower abdominal pain
incontinence or frequent urination due to Kidney deficiency
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-grade herb for severe Wind and for strengthening the Kidney in cases of impotence. It is traditionally used in formulas that tonify Kidney Yang.
precauciones: Contraindicated in Yin deficiency with rising Fire, excess ministerial Fire, Heat patterns, and Phlegm-Heat. Theoretical caution with hormonal, antihypertensive, and serotonergic medications (no documented clinical interactions).
nota: Not to be confused with noni (Morinda citrifolia).

latin: Lablab purpureus (L.) Sweet (syn. Dolichos lablab L.) (Semen Lablab Album)

indicaciones_tradicionales: chronic diarrhea due to Spleen deficiency
poor appetite and weak digestion
excessive vaginal discharge due to Spleen deficiency with Dampness
nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea due to Summer-Heat-Dampness
abdominal bloating due to Dampness
uso_historico: First appears in the Ming Yi Bie Lu as a middle-grade substance. Li Shizhen called it "the grain of the Spleen" for its affinity with digestion; it is also eaten as food in porridges and soups.
precauciones: Do not eat raw or undercooked (contains toxic lectins). Avoid during active invasion by external pathogens; excess use may cause Qi stagnation. Use caution in constipation due to Yin deficiency.
nota: Taken here as "warm" in nature (slightly warm according to the source).

acciones: expels Wind-Phlegm from the channels and the head
stops convulsions and calms internal Wind
resolves toxins and reduces swelling (external use)

aftereffects of Wind-stroke with hemiplegia
one-sided headache (migraine) due to Wind-Phlegm
tetanus
childhood convulsions and epilepsy due to Wind-Phlegm
scrofula (external use)
snakebites and stubborn ulcers (external use)
uso_historico: The name bai fu zi appears in the Ming Yi Bie Lu, although in ancient texts it probably referred to Aconitum coreanum (guan bai fu); the use of Typhonium giganteum became widespread later. It is the chief herb of the formula Qian Zheng San for facial paralysis.
precauciones: Toxic when raw: used only in processed form (zhi bai fu zi) and at controlled doses (3-6 g). Contraindicated in pregnancy and in Wind due to Yin or Blood deficiency. Use only under professional supervision.
nota: Bai fu zi can also refer to guan bai fu (Aconitum coreanum), which is more toxic; the label specifies Typhonium, so this is yu bai fu.

acciones: softens the Liver and relieves pain
indicaciones_tradicionales: irregular menstruation, painful periods, and uterine bleeding due to Blood deficiency
pallor and fatigue due to Blood deficiency
muscle cramps and spasms
spasmodic abdominal pain
pain in the flanks due to Liver Qi stagnation
headache and dizziness due to rising Liver Yang
spontaneous sweating and night sweats
uso_historico: The Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing describes shao yao for abdominal pain caused by pathogenic factors and for Blood obstruction; the formal distinction between bai shao (white, peeled) and chi shao (red) was established around the Song dynasty. Zhang Zhongjing's Shao Yao Gan Cao Tang is the classic antispasmodic formula.
precauciones: Avoid in internal Cold patterns with Yang deficiency; it may retain external pathogens. Incompatible with Li Lu (Veratrum) according to traditional rules.
nota: "Peony root without bark" corresponds to bai shao (peeled root); with the bark it would be chi shao. Some sources classify it as slightly cold.
etiquetas: peony root without bark (Chinese peony root without bark)

acciones: tonifies the Spleen and augments Qi
dries Dampness and promotes water metabolism
stabilizes the exterior and stops sweating

abdominal bloating due to Spleen deficiency with Dampness

restless fetus (threatened miscarriage) due to Spleen deficiency
uso_historico: 'Zhu' is listed in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing; the distinction between bai zhu and cang zhu was made later. It is a core ingredient of classic formulas such as Si Jun Zi Tang and Shen Ling Bai Zhu San.
precauciones: Avoid in Yin deficiency with Heat, intense thirst from injured fluids, and Qi stagnation with bloating. May potentiate omeprazole; use caution with anticoagulants and diuretics.

categoria_mtc: nourishes the Heart and calms the spirit

moistens the intestines and eases bowel movements
stops sweating due to Yin deficiency

uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-class tonic. It is an ingredient of the classic formula Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan for insomnia and palpitations due to Yin deficiency.
precauciones: Avoid with loose stools or diarrhea, copious Phlegm, and Stomach deficiency with a tendency toward nausea. May cause nausea; defatted seeds are better tolerated.

latin: Glehnia littoralis Fr. Schmidt ex Miq. (Radix Glehniae)
acciones: nourishes Lung Yin and clears Lung Heat
nourishes Stomach Yin and generates fluids
indicaciones_tradicionales: dry, unproductive cough or cough with scanty phlegm due to Heat injuring Lung Yin
dry throat and hoarse voice
dry mouth and persistent thirst
Stomach Yin deficiency or depleted fluids after febrile illnesses

irritability from Heat with injured fluids
uso_historico: The term sha shen appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing, but there it probably refers to the southern species (nan sha shen, Adenophora); bei sha shen (Glehnia) was distinguished as a separate herb in later materia medica (Ming-Qing dynasties). It is traditionally used for chronic dry cough and thirst due to Lung and Stomach Yin deficiency.
precauciones: Contraindicated in cough due to Wind-Cold, in Cold from Lung and Stomach deficiency, and in accumulation of Phlegm-Dampness. Incompatible with Li Lu (Veratrum) according to traditional rules. There is no solid clinical evidence of efficacy in humans (MSKCC).

latin: Bupleurum chinense DC. / B. scorzonerifolium Willd. (Bupleuri Radix)

uso_historico: Appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-class herb. It is the chief herb of classic formulas such as Xiao Chai Hu Tang (Shang Han Lun) and Xiao Yao San.
precauciones: Contraindicated in cough due to Yin deficiency, severe Yin or fluid deficiency, and Liver Fire with rising Yang. May cause nausea at high doses; avoid prolonged use as a single herb.

acciones: clears Liver Heat and brightens the eyes
indicaciones_tradicionales: edema and scanty urination
painful, difficult urination due to Damp-Heat in the Lower Jiao
watery diarrhea due to Dampness or Summer-Heat with Dampness
red, swollen, painful eyes due to Liver Heat
blurred vision
cough with yellow phlegm due to Lung Heat
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-grade herb. It has classically been used for lin syndrome (painful urination) and for diarrhea, following the principle of 'promoting urination to firm the stools.'
precauciones: Avoid if there is no Dampness or Damp-Heat. Use caution in pregnancy, in spermatorrhea or excessive urination due to Kidney deficiency, and in states of exhaustion. May potentiate diuretics and interact with lithium.

acciones: regulates Qi and harmonizes the Middle Jiao
indicaciones_tradicionales: epigastric and abdominal distension and fullness
belching, nausea, and vomiting
poor appetite and sluggish digestion
loose stools due to Dampness in the Spleen
cough with copious phlegm and chest tightness
prevention of the stagnation caused by tonics
uso_historico: Appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing (as ju pi). Its quality is considered to improve with aging, and it is a component of classic formulas such as Er Chen Tang and Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang.
precauciones: Contraindicated in dry cough due to Yin or Qi deficiency and in nausea due to Stomach Fire. Use caution with excess Heat or fluid deficiency; prolonged use may injure the original Qi (yuan qi).
nota: 'Citrus peel' was interpreted as chen pi (Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium), as in Sun Ten-style formulas; it is the same herb as 'tangerine mature fruit rind.'

latin: Bulbus Fritillariae Cirrhosae (Fritillaria cirrhosa D. Don)
acciones: moistens the Lung and stops cough
indicaciones_tradicionales: chronic dry cough due to Lung Yin deficiency
cough with scanty sputum that is hard to expectorate
blood-streaked sputum
cough due to Phlegm-Heat
chest tightness due to Qi stagnation with Phlegm
Phlegm-Fire nodules and scrofula
breast and lung abscesses
uso_historico: Bei Mu appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing; the distinction between Chuan Bei Mu and Zhe Bei Mu was established in Ming-Qing dynasty texts (e.g., Ben Cao Gang Mu Shi Yi). It has traditionally been used for chronic dry cough, often powdered and taken with pear.
precauciones: Not indicated for Phlegm-Cold, Phlegm-Dampness, or Phlegm-Wind. Use with caution in pregnancy and in digestive weakness (Deficiency-Cold of the Spleen and Stomach). Incompatible with Wu Tou and Fu Zi (aconite).
nota: The label says only 'fritillaria bulb'; Chuan Bei Mu (Fritillaria cirrhosa) is assumed, as it is the form most commonly used for chronic cough. It could also be Zhe Bei Mu (Fritillaria thunbergii), which is cold in nature and better suited to acute Phlegm-Heat and nodules.

latin: Rhizoma Chuanxiong (Ligusticum chuanxiong Hort.; sin. Ligusticum wallichii)

headache due to Wind-Cold, Wind-Heat, or Blood stasis
Bi syndrome (joint pain due to Wind-Dampness)

skin disorders due to Wind
uso_historico: Appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing. Traditionally considered a key herb for headaches and a gynecological mainstay as a component of the formula Si Wu Tang for regulating Blood and menstruation.
precauciones: Avoid in Yin deficiency with Heat signs and in headaches due to rising Liver Yang or Qi deficiency. Use with caution in pregnancy, heavy menstruation, and bleeding disorders. Possible interaction with anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs.
nota: On Nature's Sunshine labels, 'cnidium rhizome' and 'Ligusticum wallichii rhizome' refer to the same herb, chuan xiong (Ligusticum chuanxiong), not She Chuang Zi (Cnidium monnieri).

pinyin: da qing ye / ban lan gen

sore, inflamed throat, pharyngitis, and tonsillitis
mumps
flu and respiratory infections due to Wind-Heat

mouth ulcers
jaundice and hepatitis due to toxic Heat
dysentery due to Heat
uso_historico: Da qing ye first appears in the Ming Yi Bie Lu; the name ban lan gen for the root is recorded in Li Shizhen's Ben Cao Gang Mu, although the plant appeared in earlier texts. Both are traditionally used in febrile epidemics; the root gained modern notoriety as a preventive during the 1988 hepatitis A epidemic in Shanghai.
precauciones: Very cold: avoid in Cold due to Spleen and Stomach deficiency, in cold constitutions without a true Heat pattern, and in Wind-Cold colds. Avoid if allergic to Isatis products; use caution in aspirin sensitivity according to the source.
nota: The label "indigo leaves and root" is interpreted as the combination of the leaf (da qing ye) and the root (ban lan gen) of Isatis indigotica, which share the same nature and actions; the leaf is salty and bitter and also enters the Liver, while the root is only bitter (Heart, Stomach). Not to be confused with qing dai (indigo powder).

latin: Radix et Rhizoma Salviae Miltiorrhizae (Salvia miltiorrhiza)

uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-grade herb. A classic saying holds that 'dan shen alone is equal to the formula Si Wu Tang,' because it can both move and nourish the Blood.
precauciones: Contraindicated in pregnancy and in the absence of Blood stasis; use caution in bleeding disorders or heavy menstruation. May potentiate anticoagulants (warfarin) and antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel) and interfere with digoxin measurements. Traditionally incompatible with li lu (Veratrum).

acciones: invigorates Blood and disperses Cold to relieve pain
moistens the intestines and eases bowel movements

uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a middle-grade herb. It is the most important gynecological herb in the Chinese tradition and is part of Si Wu Tang, Dang Gui Bu Xue Tang, and many other formulas.
precauciones: Avoid with diarrhea or abdominal bloating due to Dampness, Yin deficiency with Heat, and in the early stages of a cold. May potentiate anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs (warfarin, heparin, aspirin, clopidogrel). Use caution in pregnancy and in hormone-sensitive cancers.

uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing (under the entry for gou qi) for Heat in the center and wasting-thirst. It is an ingredient of Xie Bai San, together with Sang Bai Pi, for cough due to Lung Heat.
precauciones: Avoid in Cold due to Spleen and Stomach deficiency with loose stools and in exterior Wind-Cold patterns or fever from external attack. Use with caution in pregnancy (uterotonic activity has been reported).

high blood pressure
uso_historico: Classified as a superior herb in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing. It is traditionally used as a chief herb for low back pain due to Kidney deficiency and to stabilize pregnancy.
precauciones: Contraindicated in Yin deficiency with Heat. Antagonizes Xuan Shen. Use caution with antihypertensives due to an additive blood-pressure-lowering effect.

migraine

precauciones: Contraindicated in spasms due to Blood deficiency, Yin deficiency with Heat, headache due to rising Liver Yang, and sweating due to Qi deficiency.

acciones: calms the Heart and quiets the spirit

uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-grade herb suitable for long-term use. It is one of the most widely used substances in the Chinese pharmacopeia, surpassed in frequency only by licorice.
precauciones: Non-toxic. Use with caution in excessive urination or urinary incontinence, dehydration, profuse sweating, and Yin deficiency with depleted fluids. Use caution if taken together with pharmaceutical diuretics.

uso_historico: Fu Ling appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing; Fu Shen was distinguished as a separate portion in the Ming Yi Bie Lu. It is traditionally used in formulas such as Gui Pi Tang to calm the spirit in patterns of Heart and Spleen deficiency.
precauciones: Considered very safe, with no major contraindications. Use with caution in excessive urination or Yin deficiency without Dampness.

latin: Glycyrrhiza uralensis Fisch. (Radix et Rhizoma Glycyrrhizae)

uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-grade herb. Called "Guo Lao" (the Elder of the State) for its harmonizing function, it is the most frequently used herb in classic Chinese formulas.
precauciones: Glycyrrhizin can cause pseudoaldosteronism (sodium and water retention, potassium loss, high blood pressure) at high doses or with prolonged use; in severe cases, arrhythmias. Avoid in high blood pressure, low potassium, edema, heart failure, and severe kidney disease. Interacts with digoxin and other cardiac glycosides, diuretics, antihypertensives, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, and CYP3A4 substrates. High intake during pregnancy is associated with preterm birth (NCCIH). Traditionally incompatible with Gan Sui, Da Ji, Yuan Hua, and Hai Zao.

precauciones: Contraindicated in Yin deficiency with Heat, excess Heat, vomiting due to Stomach Fire, and diarrhea due to Heat. In weak constitutions, combine with tonics to reduce its irritating effect.

precauciones: Avoid in Cold due to Spleen and Stomach deficiency, exterior deficiency with excessive sweating, marked Yin deficiency, and vomiting due to Stomach Cold. Possible interactions with anticoagulants (warfarin), diabetes medications (additive effect), CYP450 substrates, and methotrexate.

uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-grade herb suitable for long-term use. In the Ben Cao Gang Mu, Li Shizhen noted that the best medicinal berries came from Ningxia; it is part of Qi Ju Di Huang Wan for the eyes.
precauciones: Avoid with warfarin (documented cases of increased INR and bleeding). Use caution with blood-sugar-lowering medications. Avoid during acute febrile illnesses with an exterior pattern and in Spleen deficiency with loose stools. High in potassium: use caution in kidney failure.

uso_historico: Recorded in the Ming Yi Bie Lu, initially for childhood convulsions. It is the chief herb, together with Tian Ma, of the formula Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin (sold commercially as 'Gambir Formula') for rising Liver Yang.
precauciones: Use with caution if there is no true Heat or Liver Wind. Do not boil for more than 20 minutes (add near the end of the decoction). May potentiate antihypertensives and sedatives.
nota: 'Gambir' on these labels corresponds to Gou Teng (Uncaria rhynchophylla), not Uncaria gambir (gambier from Indonesia/Malaysia, used as an astringent). The commercial 'Gambir Formula' is Tian Ma Gou Teng Yin.

uso_historico: First recorded in the Yao Xing Lun (Tang dynasty). Its name means 'mender of broken bones,' reflecting its traditional use in traumatology for fractures and tendon injuries.
precauciones: Avoid in Yin deficiency with Heat, Blood deficiency without stasis, and Wind-Dryness. Use with caution in pregnancy.

uso_historico: The germinated grain appears in the Ming Yi Bie Lu under the name nie mi; the Ben Cao Gang Mu records its use. The Ben Jing Feng Yuan (Qing) notes that, unlike Mai Ya, it can supplement the Middle Jiao, making it gentler for delicate digestion.
precauciones: Avoid prolonged use without true food stagnation. Some sources indicate it may reduce breast milk production, so it is not recommended while breastfeeding. No drug interactions are known.
nota: "Oryza fruit" is interpreted as germinated rice (dao ya, Oryza sativa), called gu ya in Western literature. In the mainland Chinese pharmacopeia, gu ya refers to germinated millet (Setaria italica), which is warm in nature; dao ya (rice) is neutral. Sources differ on the first classical text (Ming Yi Bie Lu vs. Ben Cao Gang Mu).

uso_historico: Cinnamon (gui) is recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing; the use of the twig appears in the formulas of Zhang Zhongjing's Shang Han Lun, such as Gui Zhi Tang. It is one of the most widely used herbs in the classical tradition.
precauciones: Contraindicated in febrile illnesses due to Heat and in Yin deficiency with Heat. Use caution in pregnancy and with heavy menstruation. May interact with diuretics.

latin: Radix Polygoni Multiflori (Polygonum multiflorum Thunb.; sin. Reynoutria multiflora)
nombre_es: fo-ti (he shou wu, Chinese knotweed root)

uso_historico: First appears in Tang dynasty literature and was included in the Kai Bao Ben Cao (Song dynasty). The legend of Mr. He, whose gray hair turned black again, made it famous as a tonic for longevity and the hair.
precauciones: Contraindicated in Spleen deficiency with Phlegm or Dampness and in diarrhea or loose stools. Documented risk of liver toxicity (acute liver injury, sometimes severe or fatal); contraindicated in liver disease; monitor liver function and do not reintroduce after a reaction. Traditionally avoided with onion, chives, garlic, and turnip.
nota: Fo-ti is the trade name for He Shou Wu; the label does not indicate whether it is raw (sheng) or prepared (zhi).

acciones: opens the channels and unblocks menstruation
indicaciones_tradicionales: absent menstruation due to Blood stasis
painful periods
postpartum abdominal pain due to stasis and retained lochia
abdominal masses due to stasis
chest pain due to Blood stasis
bruises and pain from traumatic injury
sores and swellings due to stasis
measles rash that does not come out fully (due to stasis and Heat)
uso_historico: Mentioned as hong lan hua in the Jin Gui Yao Lue (Han dynasty) and formally recorded in the Kai Bao Ben Cao. In small doses it is considered to harmonize the Blood, and in large doses to break up stasis.
precauciones: Contraindicated in pregnancy. Avoid in bleeding disorders, excessive menstruation, and peptic ulcer; overdose may cause continuous bleeding. Use caution with anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin) and antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel).

latin: Magnolia officinalis Rehd. et Wils. (Cortex Magnoliae Officinalis)
parte: bark (of the trunk, branches, and root)
acciones: directs Qi downward and relieves distension
indicaciones_tradicionales: abdominal distension and fullness due to Dampness or Qi stagnation
food stagnation with constipation
nausea and vomiting due to Dampness in the Middle Jiao
poor appetite with a feeling of heaviness in the upper abdomen
cough and asthma with copious phlegm and chest tightness
feeling of a lump in the throat (plum-pit Qi)
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing. Zhang Zhongjing used it extensively in formulas such as Da Cheng Qi Tang and Ban Xia Hou Po Tang, the latter for the sensation of a foreign body in the throat.
precauciones: Avoid in pregnancy, Yin deficiency with Heat, Qi or Blood deficiency, diarrhea due to Heat, and postpartum Blood deficiency. May potentiate sedatives.

categoria_mtc: heavy substances that anchor and calm the spirit (Shen)
acciones: calms the spirit and stops palpitations
indicaciones_tradicionales: anxiety, insomnia, palpitations, and disturbed dreams
childhood convulsions and epilepsy
absent menstruation and abdominal pain due to Blood stasis
abdominal masses
urinary retention and painful or bloody urination (lin syndrome)
sores and skin ulcers (external use)
uso_historico: First recorded in the Ming Yi Bie Lu. It has traditionally been used in powder form to calm the spirit and for painful urination with blood or stones.
precauciones: Contraindicated in Yin deficiency with Heat and in frequent urination without stasis or Dampness. Do not decoct: it is taken as a powder or in pills (1.5-3 g). May potentiate the sedative effect of barbiturates.

nombre_es: Sichuan pepper (zanthoxylum pericarp, prickly ash peel)
nombre_en: Sichuan pepper (zanthoxylum pericarp, prickly ash peel)
acciones: warms the Middle Jiao and relieves pain
indicaciones_tradicionales: epigastric and abdominal pain due to Cold
vomiting due to Cold in the Stomach
diarrhea due to Cold or Cold-Dampness
abdominal pain due to roundworms (intestinal parasites)
eczema and itchy skin (in external washes)
vulvar itching (external washes)
uso_historico: The Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing records varieties of this pepper (qin jiao and shu jiao). It is classically used in Da Jian Zhong Tang for abdominal pain due to Cold and in Wu Mei Wan for parasites.
precauciones: Contraindicated in Yin deficiency with internal Heat and in Heat or Fire patterns. Avoid in pregnancy. Mildly toxic: overdose may cause nausea, dizziness, and convulsions.
nota: Its nature is given as warm in some sources (Me & Qi) and hot in others (Bensky, Chinese Pharmacopoeia).

acciones: drains Damp-Heat, especially from the Lower Jiao
drains Kidney Fire and clears deficiency Heat
resolves Fire toxicity and reduces skin inflammation
indicaciones_tradicionales: yellow, foul-smelling vaginal discharge due to Damp-Heat
foul-smelling diarrhea and dysentery due to Damp-Heat
painful, cloudy urination (lin syndrome due to Damp-Heat)
jaundice due to Damp-Heat
red, hot, swollen leg joints
night sweats and afternoon fever due to Yin deficiency with Fire
spermatorrhea due to Kidney deficiency Fire
sores, toxic ulcers, and oozing skin lesions (internal and external use)
uso_historico: Appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing under the name bo mu (檗木). It is traditionally used as a chief herb for Damp-Heat in the Lower Jiao and, combined with zhi mu, for Kidney deficiency Fire (e.g., in Zhi Bai Di Huang Wan).
precauciones: Contraindicated in deficiency and Cold of the Spleen and Stomach, Yang deficiency, and diarrhea without Heat. Very bitter and cold: prolonged use may injure the Stomach. Contains berberine, so interactions with drugs metabolized by liver enzymes are possible.

latin: Rhizoma Polygonati (Polygonatum sibiricum / Polygonatum kingianum / Polygonatum cyrtonema)
acciones: tonifies Spleen Qi and nourishes Stomach Yin
moistens the Lung and nourishes Lung Yin
tonifies the Kidney and strengthens Essence (Jing)
indicaciones_tradicionales: fatigue and poor appetite due to Spleen Qi deficiency
dry mouth and poor appetite due to Stomach Yin deficiency
dry cough due to Lung Yin deficiency
low back and knee pain and weakness due to Kidney deficiency
dizziness and premature graying due to Essence deficiency
thirst and wasting (xiao ke)
uso_historico: First recorded in the Ming Yi Bie Lu, which classifies it as a superior-grade herb. In the Taoist tradition it was eaten as a tonic food to prolong life and as a substitute for grains.
precauciones: Being rich and moist, it favors Dampness: contraindicated with excess Dampness, diarrhea due to Cold, fullness in the Middle Jiao, and cough with Phlegm-Heat or copious phlegm.
nota: Ambiguous name: Polygonatum can also refer to yu zhu (玉竹, Polygonatum odoratum). Huang jing was chosen because it is the Polygonatum rhizome most commonly used as a tonic in commercial formulas.

indicaciones_tradicionales: dysentery and diarrhea due to Damp-Heat
vomiting due to Stomach Heat
high fever with irritability or delirium
insomnia and irritability due to Heart Fire
mouth ulcers and sore gums
red, inflamed eyes
boils, abscesses, and toxic skin lesions
bleeding (nosebleeds, vomiting blood) due to Heat in the Blood
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing. It is one of the most bitter and cold herbs in the materia medica, classically used for Damp-Heat dysentery and to drain Heart and Stomach Fire (e.g., in Huang Lian Jie Du Tang).
precauciones: Contraindicated in Yang deficiency, Cold patterns, Qi or Blood deficiency, and Cold due to Spleen and Stomach deficiency. Prolonged use or high doses may injure the Spleen, Stomach, and Yin. Contains berberine: possible interactions with drugs metabolized by CYP450 and with cyclosporine; avoid in pregnancy and in newborns (risk of kernicterus).

latin: Astragalus membranaceus (Fisch.) Bunge / A. mongholicus (Astragali Radix)
acciones: strengthens defensive Qi (Wei Qi) and stabilizes the exterior
indicaciones_tradicionales: fatigue and poor appetite due to Spleen Qi deficiency
chronic diarrhea due to Spleen deficiency
organ prolapse (uterus, rectum, stomach) due to sinking Qi
spontaneous sweating due to defensive Qi deficiency
frequent colds
edema due to deficiency
chronic ulcers that do not heal
numbness and pain due to Qi and Blood deficiency
uso_historico: Appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-class tonic. It is the foundation of classic formulas such as Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang, Yu Ping Feng San, and Dang Gui Bu Xue Tang.
precauciones: Contraindicated in the early stages of sores, lesions with toxic Heat, exterior excess, Qi stagnation, Yin deficiency with Heat, excess Heat, and obstruction by Dampness. Use caution in late pregnancy. May interact with immunosuppressants.

acciones: cools the Blood and stops bleeding
clears Heat and calms the fetus
indicaciones_tradicionales: diarrhea and dysentery due to Damp-Heat
jaundice due to Damp-Heat
painful urination due to Damp-Heat
high fever with thirst and cough with thick yellow phlegm due to Lung Heat
alternating fever and chills (Shao Yang pattern)
bleeding due to Heat (nosebleeds, coughing up blood, blood in the stool, uterine bleeding)
restless fetus (threatened miscarriage) due to Heat
boils and toxic inflammations
headache, irritability, and red eyes due to rising Liver Yang
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a middle-grade herb. It is a core component of classic Shang Han Lun formulas such as Xiao Chai Hu Tang and Huang Qin Tang.
precauciones: Avoid in deficiency Cold and diarrhea due to Cold; use caution in Blood deficiency, edema due to Spleen deficiency, or loose stools due to Kidney deficiency. Traditionally considered to be antagonized by mu dan pi and li lu. Cases of liver injury have been reported with products containing skullcap.

latin: Agastache rugosa / Pogostemon cablin (Agastaches seu Pogostemonis Herba)
acciones: releases the exterior and clears Summer-Heat
harmonizes the Middle Jiao and stops vomiting
indicaciones_tradicionales: epigastric distension and poor appetite due to turbid Dampness in the Middle Jiao
nausea and vomiting due to Dampness
morning sickness in pregnancy
summer colds with Damp-Heat (fever, heaviness, diarrhea)
diarrhea due to Dampness
fungal infections of the hands and feet (topical use)
uso_historico: Recorded since the Ming Yi Bie Lu. It is one of the classic aromatic herbs for Summer-Dampness and digestive upsets with nausea and diarrhea.
precauciones: Contraindicated in Yin deficiency with signs of Heat and in Stomach Fire.
nota: In TCM, the name huo xiang covers both Pogostemon cablin (guang huo xiang) and Agastache rugosa (tu huo xiang); 'agastache tops' corresponds to Agastache rugosa.

acciones: tonifies Qi and strengthens the Spleen
indicaciones_tradicionales: fatigue and tiredness due to Qi deficiency
poor appetite due to Spleen Qi deficiency
cough with phlegm and chronic bronchitis
insomnia and agitation
elevated blood lipids (modern use)
elevated blood sugar (modern use)
high blood pressure (modern use)
uso_historico: First recorded in the Jiu Huang Ben Cao (1406) as a famine food; its medicinal use is documented in the Ben Cao Gang Mu (1578). It became popular as a tonic tea in southern China and came to be called "southern ginseng" after Japanese studies in the 1970s found saponins similar to those in ginseng.
precauciones: Avoid in Cold due to Spleen and Stomach deficiency with diarrhea and in pregnancy. Use caution with anticoagulants, antihypertensives, and blood-sugar-lowering medications due to possible additive effects.

acciones: expels Phlegm and benefits the throat
directs the action of other herbs to the upper body
indicaciones_tradicionales: cough with copious phlegm or phlegm that is hard to expectorate (due to Cold or Heat)
sore throat
hoarseness or loss of voice
feeling of tightness in the chest
lung abscess with purulent sputum
throat abscesses
uso_historico: Appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing. It is considered the 'messenger' herb that carries other substances to the chest; it is the basis of the classic formula Jie Geng Tang (with gan cao) from the Shang Han Lun for sore throat.
precauciones: Avoid in chronic cough due to Yin deficiency, in coughing up blood, and in rising Qi (nausea, vomiting). High doses may cause nausea and vomiting; its saponins have a hemolytic effect if injected.

acciones: cools the Blood and stops dysentery
indicaciones_tradicionales: Wind-Heat colds and flu with fever
early stages of febrile illnesses due to Heat
sore, inflamed throat
abscesses, boils, and skin sores due to toxic Heat
mastitis
bloody dysentery due to toxic Heat
Summer-Heat conditions
uso_historico: Appears in the Ming Yi Bie Lu under the name Ren Dong (忍冬), classified as superior grade; the name jin yin hua ("gold and silver flower") became widespread in the Ming era and appears in the Ben Cao Gang Mu. It is the chief herb of Yin Qiao San for Wind-Heat.
precauciones: Avoid in Spleen and Stomach Yang deficiency, Wind-Cold patterns, and Qi deficiency with thin, watery pus; do not use long-term without signs of Heat.

parte: flower spike (jing jie sui) / aerial parts
acciones: releases the exterior and expels Wind
indicaciones_tradicionales: Wind-Cold or Wind-Heat colds with fever, chills, and headache
sore throat with Wind invasion
early-stage measles with incomplete rash
hives and itchy skin due to Wind
early-stage boils with chills and fever
bleeding (nosebleeds, bloody stools, uterine bleeding) when used charred
postpartum spasms
uso_historico: Appears in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing under the name jia su (假苏). It is valued as a gentle exterior-releasing herb, useful for both Wind-Cold and Wind-Heat, and is part of formulas such as Jing Fang Bai Du San and Yin Qiao San.
precauciones: Avoid when measles has fully erupted, with open sores, spontaneous sweating, or headache due to Yin deficiency or internal Wind. Do not use in the absence of pathogenic Wind. Do not boil for a long time (volatile oils).
nota: The flower spike (jing jie sui) is considered more potent than the stem for expelling Wind from the exterior.

categoria_mtc: releases the exterior: pungent and cool (disperses Wind-Heat)
acciones: calms the Liver and brightens the eyes
moderates Liver Yang and extinguishes Wind
indicaciones_tradicionales: Wind-Heat colds with fever and headache
red, swollen, sore eyes
dry eyes and blurred vision due to Liver and Kidney Yin deficiency
dizziness and headache due to rising Liver Yang
high blood pressure with headache (modern use)
boils and toxic swellings
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-class herb. It is traditionally taken as a tea; the white variety is preferred for nourishing the Liver and brightening the eyes, and the yellow variety for dispersing Wind-Heat.
precauciones: Avoid high doses in Qi deficiency, poor appetite, Stomach Cold, or diarrhea. Contraindicated in Yang deficiency or Cold patterns. Possible allergy in people sensitive to the Asteraceae (daisy) family.

acciones: moistens the Lung and directs Qi downward
indicaciones_tradicionales: acute or chronic cough of any kind, especially due to Cold
wheezing and chronic asthma
chronic bronchitis
smoker's cough
cough with blood-tinged sputum (in combination, with caution)
lung abscess with purulent sputum
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a middle-grade herb. It is traditionally used honey-toasted to moisten the Lung and is often combined with zi wan for chronic cough.
precauciones: Avoid in cough due to Heat or Yin deficiency; use caution with bloody or purulent cough. Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that are potentially toxic to the liver: avoid prolonged use or high doses. High doses may cause fainting and apnea.

indicaciones_tradicionales: Wind-Heat colds with fever and sore throat
early stages of febrile illnesses
boils, carbuncles, and abscesses

irritability and fever due to Heat in the Heart
painful urination and blood in the urine due to Heat
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing. It is traditionally called 'the sacred herb for sores' and is a key component, together with Jin Yin Hua, of Yin Qiao San for Wind-Heat infections.
precauciones: Contraindicated in Spleen and Stomach deficiency with loose stools, in open sores that have already drained, and in patterns of Yin deficiency with Heat.

acciones: strengthens the Spleen and stops diarrhea
benefits the Kidney and secures Essence
nourishes the Heart and calms the spirit
indicaciones_tradicionales: chronic diarrhea and poor appetite due to Spleen deficiency
seminal emissions and premature ejaculation due to Kidney deficiency
excessive vaginal discharge
frequent urination
insomnia, palpitations, and restlessness due to Heart-Kidney disharmony
anxiety
uso_historico: Recorded in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing as a superior-grade herb; the name lian zi appears in Tao Hongjing's Ben Cao Jing Ji Zhu. It is a key ingredient of Shen Ling Bai Zhu San for diarrhea due to Spleen deficiency and is also eaten as food.
precauciones: Avoid in constipation or dry stools, food stagnation, acute Heat patterns, and Yin deficiency with dryness.

parte: fruiting body (the label 'reishi mushroom mycelia' refers to the mycelium)
categoria_mtc: nourishes the Heart and calms the spirit
acciones: tonifies Heart Qi and Blood and calms the spirit
transforms Phlegm and stops cough and wheezing
indicaciones_tradicionales: insomnia due to Heart deficiency
palpitations
poor memory and forgetfulness
anxiety and restlessness
chronic cough and wheezing due to deficiency or Phlegm-Dampness
fatigue and weakness due to consumptive deficiency
shortness of breath and poor appetite due to deficiency
uso_historico: Classified as a superior substance in the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing, which describes six types according to color. It was traditionally called the 'mushroom of immortality' and used as a tonic for longevity and to calm the spirit.
precauciones: Use with caution in excess patterns. May cause skin rashes, diarrhea, dry mouth, or flushing. May potentiate anticoagulants/antiplatelet drugs, antihypertensives, and immunosuppressants; cases of liver toxicity have been reported with powdered preparations. Traditionally incompatible with Chang Shan and Yin Chen Hao.
nota: This entry also covers 'reishi mushroom mycelia'; the traditional information refers to the fruiting body, and the mycelium may differ in composition.
